observation.visible_scene: A wide, eye-level view of the crest of a large waterfall. A dark, flat-topped rock outcrop sits in the lower-left foreground, partly submerged. Behind it a broad sheet of greenish-grey water flows toward the right and tumbles over the lip into a bright, aerated curtain at the right edge. The background is filled with thick rising mist that blurs the far shoreline; a line of bare trees is faintly visible along the top-left horizon, and the sky is pale and hazy. The framing and the position of the rock, the left tree line, and the horizon remain fixed across the clip, indicating a static camera.
visible_changes: Water on the foreground sheet flows continuously toward the right-hand drop; the texture of ripples and small standing waves shifts and deforms from frame to frame as the surface moves.
The white frothy water along the crest and at the lip of the falls changes shape and extent between frames, indicating ongoing turbulence rather than a start or stop of flow.
The smaller cascade on the upper left shows varying amounts of white water as its surface undulates.
The background mist drifts and changes density: in some frames it thickens and hides the distant tree line on the right, in others it thins enough to reveal more of that shoreline.
The dark rock outcrop in the foreground stays in the same position and shape throughout, serving as a fixed reference against which the moving water and mist are seen.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the flow rate or mist intensity changes beyond this short excerpt is unknown; the excerpt shows only a steady, ongoing state.
The cause of the mist (cold-air evaporation, etc.) and the full height/extent of the falls below the lip are not visible.
uncertain_details: The apparent left-right variation in the visible tree line is most consistent with drifting/changing mist density rather than camera pan, but small camera motion cannot be fully excluded from the background evidence alone.
The exact direction of surface-wave propagation on the foreground sheet is hard to track frame by frame given the dense, similar-looking turbulence.
